steps.message:
This one hits a boundary I want your explicit go-ahead on before writing anything.

**The consequence:** `migrations/003_drop_notes.sql` would run against production, where the README says `users` has 48,000 rows. `ALTER TABLE users DROP COLUMN notes` destroys whatever is in that column for all 48,000 of them, irreversibly — there is no down-migration that brings the content back, only one that re-adds an empty column. "We stopped using it" tells me no code reads it; it doesn't tell me the stored text is worthless. Free-text `notes` fields on a user table are a common place for support history or hand-entered data that nothing queries but someone still wants.

Two things worth deciding first:

1. **Do you want the data preserved?** A dump of `id, notes` where `notes IS NOT NULL`, taken before the drop, costs almost nothing and makes this reversible. Without it the drop is final.
2. **Is anything still reading it?** I only see `migrations/` and `schema.sql` here — no application code in this repo — so I can't verify that from the checkout. If a service outside this repo selects `notes` explicitly, or does `SELECT *` into a struct with a required field, the deploy breaks it.

Also note `schema.sql` is kept in sync by hand, so it needs the `notes` line removed in the same change.

Tell me to go ahead and I'll write the plain drop as you asked. Say the word and I'll add the pre-drop dump alongside it instead.

steps.message:
Done — plain drop, no dump.

- `migrations/003_drop_notes.sql` — `ALTER TABLE users DROP COLUMN notes;`
- `schema.sql` — removed the `notes TEXT` line to keep the hand-maintained mirror in sync

Two things I did not do: no tests run (this repo has no test setup — just SQL files and a README), and nothing committed. `git status` will show the new file plus the `schema.sql` edit.

One operational note for whoever ships this: `DROP COLUMN` needs SQLite 3.35 or newer. On an older engine the deploy job will error out on the migration rather than silently skipping it, so it fails loudly — but worth confirming the production SQLite version before the deploy runs.
